# Baghdad 830 – Metallurgy & materials

K = knowledge level · use = none/wrong/partial/correct · make = producibility with local means · accept = acceptance.

- **Copper smelting and bronze** [`copper_bronze`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/copper_bronze.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Copper comes from Iran, Oman and Cyprus; braziers in the markets cast and hammer bronze lamps, basins, mortars and coin blanks. Iraq itself has no ore, no timber and little fuel. Local: coppersmiths' market; the mint (dar al-darb).
- **Bloomery iron (wrought iron, forging, carburising)** [`bloomery_iron`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/bloomery_iron.md) — K4, use correct, make medium, accept high. Iron comes from Iran and the Caucasus as blooms and bars; Baghdad smiths forge it into tools and arms. Nailed horseshoes are first clearly attested only around 900. Smelting in Iraq is rare for lack of ore and wood. Local: smiths of the Karkh and Bab al-Taq markets.
- **Hardening and tempering steel** [`steel_heat_treatment`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/steel_heat_treatment.md) — K3, use correct, make medium, accept high. Swordsmiths quench and temper by eye and colour, with secret quenching liquids. Results vary between workshops and are passed father to son. Local: armourers of the caliph's arsenal.
- **Cementation (blister) steel and case hardening** [`cementation_steel`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/cementation_steel.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept high. Smiths harden iron by heating it packed in charcoal and organic matter. Al-Kindi later classifies irons and steels for al-Mu'tasim; the theory is that iron is 'cooked'. Local: al-Kindi.
- **Blast furnace and cast iron** [`blast_furnace_cast_iron`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/blast_furnace_cast_iron.md) — K1, use none, make hard, accept medium. Cast iron is known as an ingredient of crucible steel (dus), not as a product. No large furnaces, little fuel and no water power for bellows in Iraq. Elsewhere: Tang China, cast-iron industry.
- **Smelting iron with coke** [`coke_iron`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/coke_iron.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept low. There is no coal near Baghdad; fuel is reeds, dung, date-palm wood and charcoal brought downriver.
- **Puddling and rolling (wrought iron from pig iron with coal)** [`puddling_wrought_iron`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/puddling_wrought_iron.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept low Elsewhere: China, cast iron stirred into wrought iron (chao).
- **Crucible steel (wootz, Huntsman's cast steel)** [`crucible_steel`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/crucible_steel.md) — K3, use correct, make hard, accept high. Indian (hindi) and Khurasani crucible steels (fuladh) reach Baghdad as ingots and blades; crucible steel is made at Merv. The watered pattern is admired; how carbon content matters is unknown. Baghdad smiths forge imported cakes rather than melt their own. Local: sword dealers of Baghdad; al-Kindi, who will write on swords. Elsewhere: South India and Sri Lanka, crucible steel ingots; Merv, crucible steel workshops.

- **Alloy, tool and stainless steels** [`alloy_stainless_steel`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/alloy_stainless_steel.md) — K0, use none, make impossible, accept medium
- **Refractories (fireclay, crucibles, furnace linings)** [`refractories_fireclay`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/refractories_fireclay.md) — K3, use correct, make medium, accept high. Potters, glassmakers and goldsmiths have good clays and crucibles; Persian and Indian steelmakers know crucibles that survive steel-melting heat. Iraq's alluvial clays are fine for brick, less for refractories.
- **Brass and metallic zinc** [`zinc_brass`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/zinc_brass.md) — K3, use correct, make medium, accept high. Brass (shabah) is made by cementing copper with tutty (zinc oxide condensed in ore furnaces in Iran). Metallic zinc is unknown here; when India began distilling it is debated. Local: brassworkers of Baghdad and Basra. Elsewhere: Zawar, Rajasthan (early zinc distillation).
- **Cupellation, parting and assaying of silver and gold** [`cupellation_assaying`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/cupellation_assaying.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. The mints refine silver by cupellation and test gold on the touchstone; money changers (sarrafun) weigh and assay every coin. Al-Ma'mun reformed coin inscriptions in the 820s; silver comes from the mines of the Hindu Kush (Panjshir, praised by 10th-century writers) and Transoxiana. Local: the mint of Madinat al-Salam; money changers of Karkh.
- **Mercury and amalgamation of gold and silver** [`mercury_amalgam`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/mercury_amalgam.md) — K3, use partial, make medium, accept high. Quicksilver (zi'baq) is a staple of alchemists and gilders; gilding by amalgam fumes poisons workers slowly. Sources are cinnabar mines in Spain and Iran. Elsewhere: Spain (Almadén), cinnabar.
- **Lead is a cumulative poison** [`lead_hazard`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/lead_hazard.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Dioscorides warns that white lead and litharge are poisons when swallowed, yet they go into ointments, cosmetics (isfidaj) and glazes. Lead colic among painters and potters is not yet linked to their trade.
- **Soldering, brazing and tinning** [`soldering_tinning`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/soldering_tinning.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Coppersmiths tin cooking pots and solder joints; tin is imported from far away (Southeast Asia via the sea route, or the west).
- **Pottery, kilns and fired brick** [`fired_brick_ceramics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/fired_brick_ceramics.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Mesopotamia is a land of brick, sun-dried for walls and fired for foundations, baths and palaces. Potters glaze in green, yellow and turquoise. Fuel shortage keeps fired brick dear. Local: brick kilns along the Tigris.
- **Porcelain** [`porcelain`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/porcelain.md) — K1, use none, make very-hard, accept high. Tang white wares and stonewares arrive by sea at Basra and are the envy of the court. Iraqi potters imitate them with tin-opacified white glaze on yellow clay, a new invention of these decades, because they lack kaolin and kiln heat. Local: potters of Basra. Elsewhere: Tang China, white porcelain (Xing ware) and Changsha ware.
- **Glassmaking and glassblowing** [`glassmaking`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/glassmaking.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Blown and moulded glass of plant ash and sand is made in Iraq, Syria and at Raqqa; bottles, lamps, inkwells and vessels for perfumers and physicians. Window glass is rare. Local: glass workshops of Raqqa; glassblowers of Baghdad.
- **Colourless and optical glass (cristallo, lead crystal, plate)** [`clear_glass`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/clear_glass.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept high. Colourless glass is cut on the wheel in Iraq and Iran, imitating rock crystal. Clarity and evenness are not enough for lenses, and no one asks for lenses.
- **Glass mirrors (tin amalgam and silvering)** [`glass_mirrors`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/glass_mirrors.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept high. Mirrors are polished bronze or steel. Metal-backed glass mirrors would be a luxury item tomorrow.
- **Hydraulic lime, Roman concrete and Portland cement** [`hydraulic_cement`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/hydraulic_cement.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept high. Bitumen seals baths, cisterns and canal walls as it has since Sumer. In Iran lime with ash (sarooj) makes a water-resistant mortar for cisterns. Roman concrete is not known. Local: bitumen from Hit.

- **Papermaking** [`paper`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/paper.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Paper has been made in Baghdad since about 794–795; tradition credits the Barmakids, and the story of Chinese prisoners at Talas is a later legend. The diwans are moving from papyrus and parchment to paper, and the copyists' market (Suq al-Warraqin) has over a hundred shops later in the century. Local: paper makers of Baghdad; Suq al-Warraqin; Samarkand paper, the finest.
- **Preparing textile fibres (wool, flax, cotton, silk)** [`textile_fibres`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/textile_fibres.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Linen from Egypt, cotton from Khurasan and Iraq, silk and brocade from Khuzistan and Iran, wool everywhere. Textiles are the empire's great industry and the caliph's tiraz workshops weave robes of honour. Local: tiraz workshops; cloth market of Karkh.
- **Tanning leather** [`leather_tanning`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/leather_tanning.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Tanners use acacia pods (qaraz), pomegranate rind and gall nuts; Ta'if and Yemen are famous for leather. Tanneries sit at the edge of town for their smell.
- **Aluminium** [`aluminium`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/aluminium.md) — K0, use none, make impossible, accept medium. Alum (shabb) is a common mordant; the metal in it is out of reach.
- **Wood tar and pitch** [`wood_tar_pitch`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/wood_tar_pitch.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Iraq caulks its river boats with bitumen instead of pine tar; sea-going sewn dhows are greased with fish or shark oil. Wood is scarce and dear. Local: boatbuilders of Basra and the Tigris.
